✦ THE HEART OF THE GROVE ✦

DeEngineering

What if we listened to the lives behind the degrees?

Engineering is often narrated through numbers: entrance ranks, grades, placements, laboratories, innovation and institutional prestige. These achievements matter. But they do not tell us what it feels like to arrive in a classroom and wonder whether we belong, to find comfort in an unexpected friendship, or to navigate expectations that were never written into a syllabus.

DeEngineering is a way of listening beyond the official story. It asks what becomes visible when students' ordinary, contradictory and deeply personal experiences are treated as knowledge rather than background noise. It does not reject engineering or the possibilities it creates. Instead, it asks how technical education might be understood more fully when care, dignity, gender, identity, power and emotional life are part of the conversation.

✿✧❀

Not just what we build.
How we live while building it.

❀

Beyond achievement

Who is celebrated by institutional histories, and whose daily labour, doubts and small victories go unnamed? The archive makes room for what rankings cannot measure.

☾

Beyond silence

Some experiences are spoken, others entrusted as notes, and some remain unshared. DeEngineering respects the choice of how—and whether—a story is told.

✧

Beyond a single story

Joy and exclusion can coexist. A person may love a subject and still feel lonely in its classrooms. These accounts resist easy conclusions and universal claims.

🌿

Toward a more caring education

Listening is not the same as fixing. But attention can make overlooked patterns harder to dismiss and open questions about what a more humane institution could become.

This is not a verdict on every engineering institution. It is a growing counter-archive: a place where lived experience can stand beside official histories, and where a student is more than a statistic.

✿ A reflection from the grove ✿

Who gets to feel like they belong?

An original editorial reflection on gender, visibility and everyday belonging in engineering education. This is not an interview or an individual participant testimony.

There is something about engineering education that we don't talk about enough: how a person can genuinely love the subject and still feel out of place in the spaces where they're supposed to learn it.

We talk so much about who cleared which exam, who got the internship, who is doing well academically. But what about the ordinary day-to-day experience of being there? Who gets invited into a group without having to ask twice? Who feels comfortable raising a question? Who can walk into a classroom without first calculating how they will be perceived?

I keep coming back to the idea that belonging isn't always about having a huge friend circle. Sometimes it's simply about not feeling invisible. It's being taken seriously when you have an idea, being allowed to make mistakes without being reduced to a stereotype, and being treated as someone who has earned their place.

And for women in male-dominated classrooms, these questions can become especially complicated. Not every uncomfortable moment is dramatic. Sometimes it's a joke you don't know how to respond to. Sometimes it's being interrupted, or feeling that you have to work twice as hard to be seen as capable. Sometimes it's just the exhaustion of constantly being aware that you're one of very few.

Aur phir hum bol dete hain, 'College life hai, adjust kar lo.' But why is adjustment always treated as an individual responsibility? Why don't we ask what the classroom, the peer group or the institution could do differently?

I don't want this reflection to suggest that every engineering classroom is the same, or that every woman experiences it in the same way. People find friendship, mentorship, joy and confidence here too. That's part of the story. The point is to make room for both realities without forcing one to cancel out the other.

For me, this is what DeEngineering is trying to do. Not reject engineering, but question the parts of its culture that make people feel small. To imagine an education where being technically good and being human aren't treated as separate things.

Because a place that teaches us how to build the future should also care about how we are living in the present.

Six enchanted pathways

Every path holds a story

Wander between clearings. Each theme connects to others, just as the stories do. Choose whichever path calls to you.

✿many paths,
one grove

Belonging

Inspired by Whisper of the Heart
“A voice becomes clearer when it is allowed to grow.”

Entering an institution is not the same as feeling welcome in it. Students may be surrounded by classmates yet feel painfully alone, uncertain about where to sit, whom to speak to or whether their questions will sound foolish. This chapter looks at the slow, uneven work of finding community: the first friend who saves you a seat, the courage to ask for help, and the relief of being recognised without having to prove yourself every day. It also asks who gets to feel at home easily, and who must work harder to belong.

Expectations & self-doubt

Inspired by Kiki’s Delivery Service
“Confidence can disappear even while our abilities remain.”

A new academic environment can turn excitement into comparison. Everyone else seems to understand the lecture, know their career plan or have a perfect routine, while you are still trying to keep up with the reading. This theme explores the pressure of grades, attendance, internships and the constant demand to appear capable. Like a young person finding her way through an unfamiliar city, students may need time, rest and kindness before they can trust their own pace again.

Power & institutional culture

Inspired by Spirited Away
“Keep hold of yourself in a world of unfamiliar rules.”

Universities have written policies, but students also encounter unwritten hierarchies: how to address seniors, where they may go, what they can wear and when they are expected to remain silent. In the most troubling accounts, humiliation is excused as tradition and reporting wrongdoing feels risky. This chapter considers how fear and conformity can be normalised, and why a culture of learning must also protect dignity, consent and the freedom to question authority.

Identity & freedom

Inspired by Howl’s Moving Castle
“You are more than the shape others expect you to take.”

An academic institution can be a place to discover yourself, but it can also impose expectations about gender, appearance, relationships and what a successful student should look like. Women in engineering may be treated as novelties rather than peers; queer students may have to calculate when it is safe to be visible. This chapter explores the difference between being tolerated and being respected, and the importance of having room to define yourself on your own terms.

Friendship & everyday joy

Inspired by My Neighbor Totoro
“A small kindness can make a strange place feel familiar.”

Not every story about education is about struggle. There are shared lunches, borrowed notes, quiet walks after class, jokes that make a difficult day lighter, and people who notice when you are missing. These ordinary moments may not appear in rankings or official histories, but they shape how students remember an institution. This chapter preserves companionship and the everyday care that helps people keep going, without pretending friendship can solve every structural problem.

Dreams & uncertain futures

Inspired by The Wind Rises
“Even uncertain futures begin with the courage to imagine.”

Students arrive carrying expectations about their future: a degree, meaningful work, financial independence, or a chance to explore a field they love. As graduation approaches, those hopes meet the realities of internships, placements, family expectations and uncertainty. This chapter asks how ambition changes with experience, how students make room for paths they had not imagined, and what it means to grow without already knowing exactly who you will become.

✧ With gratitude and accountability ✧

Acknowledgements & editorial commitments

This grove exists because people trusted us with experiences that may be joyful, complicated, painful or difficult to name.

To the people who shared

We thank every participant who chose to speak, to be heard, or to let an interviewer take notes without retaining a recording. Sharing an experience is not an obligation; choosing silence, withholding details or setting boundaries is equally deserving of respect. We recognise the time, vulnerability and emotional work involved in speaking about belonging, discrimination, institutional expectations and uncertainty.

Consent and the right to choose a format

The archive's audio contributions were collected with consent, and identifying details were removed as described by the project team. Other contributors preferred not to have their experiences kept or published as audio. For those accounts, interview notes were used to develop written narratives with permission. Consent to participate, consent to record, consent to edit and consent to publish are distinct decisions; this archive aims to respect the boundaries each contributor set.

How stories are represented

Written testimonies are not word-for-word transcripts. Some wording, sequence and identifying context have been adjusted for readability or privacy. Where an account is an adaptation of publicly shared writing rather than an interview, it is identified separately. The original editorial reflection on women in engineering is clearly distinguished from participant testimonies. It does not reproduce or claim to speak for any particular online author.

Whose stories are missing

These contributions cannot represent all students, all institutions, or the diversity of women and queer people in engineering education. Some experiences remain absent because people were not approached, did not feel safe participating, did not wish to be recorded, or chose not to share. The archive's silences are a limitation of its reach, not evidence that those experiences do not exist. We will not use a small collection to make universal claims.

Listening without spectacle

Illustration, drifting bubbles and gentle music are intended to welcome visitors, not to beautify harm or turn distress into entertainment. Music is optional and pauses during spoken recordings. Emotion bubbles are editorial excerpts or thematic phrases, not claims that a contributor said those exact words unless specifically attributed. Visitors can reduce motion and read without sound.

Responsibility beyond publication

We aim to make room for correction, clarification and withdrawal requests where feasible. We will avoid presenting unverified allegations as established findings, and we will not identify institutions or individuals unnecessarily. We recognise that anonymising names does not always eliminate the possibility of recognition through voice or context. Ongoing review is part of caring for an archive, not a one-time task.

To everyone who trusted us with a piece of their story: this archive is possible because of you. Our responsibility is to preserve the complexity of what you shared, including the parts that do not fit a neat or hopeful ending.

A note from the archive ✧

Still growing, still listening

Editorial transparency: this is a private review build. The archive is not yet cleared for public release.

Like any living archive, this grove is a work in progress. Some stories have yet to find their way here.

🌱

An archive still growing

This archive does not yet hold enough experiences to represent the diversity of women’s and queer lives in engineering institutions. The stories gathered here offer important perspectives, but they cannot speak for everyone.

🪶

Stories thoughtfully retold

Some accounts have been creatively adapted. Permission to adapt or share one account does not automatically extend to all material. Every participant-derived adaptation needs confirmation of the final wording, and original editorial commentary must be distinguished from participant testimony.

🌼

Consent, representation and correction

The collection is not representative of all women or queer students. Consent and removal of identifiers have been reported by the project team; a final contextual privacy review is still advisable; contributors should have a clear way to request corrections or withdrawal, subject to the archive’s stated policy.
